claim: In Europe, women can expect to live on average 82 years and men 75 years.
source: In Europe, women can expect to live on average 82 years and men 75 years.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general statement about current life expectancy in Europe.

claim: Life expectancy in 18 European countries will increase from, on average, 83.4 years for women and 78.3 years for men in 2014 to 92.8 years for women and 90.5 years for men in 2065.
source: We project that life expectancy in these 18 countries will increase from, on average, 83.4 years for women and 78.3 years for men in 2014 to 92.8 years for women and 90.5 years for men in 2065.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' projection methodology, based on their data analysis and modeling.

claim: The authors' projection results in higher future life expectancy values compared to Lee-Carter, Eurostat, and United Nations projections.
source: Compared to others (Lee–Carter, Eurostat, United Nations), we project higher future life expectancy values and more realistic differences between countries and sexes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparative data presented in the results section.

claim: The authors' projection results in more realistic differences between countries and sexes compared to other projection methods.
source: Compared to others (Lee–Carter, Eurostat, United Nations), we project higher future life expectancy values and more realistic differences between countries and sexes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparative analysis in the results section.

claim: The societal and academic relevance of obtaining reliable and robust mortality forecasts has increased recently.
source: Recently, the societal and academic relevance of obtaining reliable and robust mortality forecasts has increased due to the revived debate on the existence and proximity of a limit to human life expectancy (Fries, 1980; Manton et al., 1991; Couzin, 2005; de Beer et al., 2017; Olshansky and Carnes, 2019; Vaupel et al., 2021); the linkage between life expectancy developments and retirement age in many European countries (Carone et al., 2016; OECD, 2016); the stagnation of increases in life expectancy in the United States, the United Kingdom, and other European countries since 2011 (Murphy et al., 2019; Raleigh, 2019); and the recent COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature and recent events.

claim: Life expectancy has stagnated in the United States, the United Kingdom, and other European countries since 2011.
source: the stagnation of increases in life expectancy in the United States, the United Kingdom, and other European countries since 2011 (Murphy et al., 2019; Raleigh, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Murphy et al., 2019 and Raleigh, 2019.

claim: The majority of currently existing mortality forecasting methods are mainly based on extrapolations of past trends in age-specific mortality.
source: The majority of the currently existing mortality forecasting methods, including those used by statistical offices in Europe, are mainly based on extrapolations of past trends in age-specific mortality (Booth and Tickle, 2008; Stoeldraijer et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Booth and Tickle, 2008 and Stoeldraijer et al., 2013a.

claim: The stochastic Lee-Carter mortality projection methodology has long been the benchmark extrapolative mortality forecasting method.
source: The stochastic Lee–Carter mortality projection methodology (Lee and Carter, 1992) has long been the benchmark extrapolative mortality forecasting method (see Janssen, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee and Carter, 1992 and Janssen, 2018.

claim: Mechanically extrapolating past national mortality trends can result in unreliable outcomes.
source: It is, however, increasingly being acknowledged that mechanically extrapolating past national mortality trends can result in unreliable outcomes (e.g., Janssen and Kunst, 2007; Janssen et al., 2013; Bongaarts, 2014; Stoeldraijer, 2019; Li and Raftery, 2021; Blakely, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: When past trends in mortality are non-linear, the projection outcome will depend to a large extent on the period on which the extrapolation is based.
source: First, when past trends in mortality are non-linear, the projection outcome will depend to a large extent on the period on which the extrapolation is based (Janssen and Kunst, 2007; Janssen et al., 2013; Stoeldraijer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janssen and Kunst, 2007; Janssen et al., 2013; and Stoeldraijer, 2019.

claim: Extrapolative mortality forecasts made for individual populations often project unrealistic crossovers or large future differences in life expectancy between populations.
source: Second, extrapolative mortality forecasts made for individual populations often project unrealistic crossovers or large future differences in life expectancy between populations (Li and Lee, 2005; Janssen et al., 2013; Hyndman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Lee, 2005; Janssen et al., 2013; and Hyndman et al., 2013.

claim: Eastern European countries have historically had relatively low life expectancy but have experienced improvements since 2005.
source: For example, extrapolating the large mortality declines observed in Eastern European countries – which have historically had relatively low life expectancy, but have experienced improvements since 2005 (Trias-Llimós et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Trias-Llimós et al., 2018.

claim: Lifestyle factors, particularly smoking, alcohol abuse, and obesity, contributed greatly to deviations and differences in past trends in mortality and life expectancy.
source: Lifestyle factors, particularly smoking, alcohol abuse, and obesity, contributed greatly to these deviations and differences (e.g., Lhachimi et al., 2016; WHO, 2018a; Janssen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lhachimi et al., 2016; WHO, 2018a; and Janssen et al., 2021.

claim: The decelerating life expectancy improvements among men in many north-western European countries in the 1950s and 1960s can be largely explained by the smoking epidemic.
source: For example, the decelerating life expectancy improvements among men in many north-western European countries in the 1950s and 1960s, and, in later decades, in other European countries and among women, can be largely explained by the smoking epidemic (Rostron and Wilmoth, 2011; Janssen et al., 2015; Lindahl-Jacobsen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rostron and Wilmoth, 2011; Janssen et al., 2015; and Lindahl-Jacobsen et al., 2016.

claim: The pattern of a rapid increase and a subsequent decline in smoking prevalence occurred first among men in Anglo-Saxon countries, and was followed later in other countries and by women.
source: The pattern of a rapid increase and a subsequent decline in smoking prevalence occurred first among men in Anglo-Saxon countries, and was followed later in other countries and by women (Lopez et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lopez et al., 1994.

claim: Smoking prevalence patterns resulted in similar patterns in smoking-attributable mortality about 30-40 years later.
source: These developments resulted in similar patterns in smoking-attributable mortality about 30–40 years later (Lopez et al., 1994; Janssen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lopez et al., 1994 and Janssen, 2020.

claim: Large increases in alcohol consumption and alcohol-attributable mortality between 1990 and 2005 in Eastern Europe contributed to the stalling of life expectancy improvements in Eastern Europe in this period.
source: The large increases in alcohol consumption and alcohol-attributable mortality between 1990 and 2005 in Eastern Europe contributed to the stalling of life expectancy improvements in Eastern Europe in this period (Trias-Llimós et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Trias-Llimós et al., 2018.

claim: More favourable alcohol-related trends in Eastern Europe since 2005 have contributed to the convergence in life expectancy levels between Eastern and Western Europe.
source: The more favourable alcohol-related trends in Eastern Europe since 2005 have contributed to the convergence in life expectancy levels between Eastern and Western Europe.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the previous claim about alcohol trends in Eastern Europe.

claim: The stagnation in life expectancy improvements since approximately 2011 in the United States and the United Kingdom can be partly attributed to high obesity prevalence and obesity-attributable mortality in these countries.
source: The stagnation in life expectancy improvements since approximately 2011 in the United States and the United Kingdom, but also in other selected European countries (Murphy et al., 2019), can be partly attributed to the high obesity prevalence and obesity-attributable mortality in these countries (Raleigh, 2019; Janssen et al., 2020a; Janssen et al., 2020b )
evidence: This is supported by citations to Murphy et al., 2019; Raleigh, 2019; Janssen et al., 2020a; and Janssen et al., 2020b.

claim: The stagnation in life expectancy improvements since approximately 2011 can be attributed to the increasing impact on life expectancy levels of past large increases in obesity prevalence.
source: and to the increasing impact on life expectancy levels of past large increases in obesity prevalence (Vidra et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vidra et al., 2019.

claim: Previous mortality forecasts that incorporated lifestyle information generally included information on only one lifestyle factor, usually smoking.
source: Previous mortality forecasts that incorporated lifestyle information (Bongaarts, 2006; Pampel, 2005; Wang and Preston, 2009; King and Soneji, 2011; Preston et al., 2014; French and O'Hare, 2013; Foreman et al., 2018; Janssen and Kunst, 2007; Janssen et al., 2013; Li and Raftery, 2021) generally included information on only one lifestyle factor, usually smoking.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous mortality forecasting studies.

claim: Previous coherent or multi-population forecasting methods have been applied almost exclusively to all-cause mortality.
source: The previous so-called coherent or multi-population forecasting methods that take into account the mortality experiences of other countries (Li and Lee, 2005; Hyndman et al., 2013; Enchev et al., 2017; Eurostat, 2020b; Bergeron-Boucher et al., 2018) have, despite their growing popularity, so far been applied almost exclusively to all-cause mortality.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Lee, 2005; Hyndman et al., 2013; Enchev et al., 2017; Eurostat, 2020b; and Bergeron-Boucher et al., 2018.

claim: Only two previous projections incorporated both lifestyle factors and mortality experiences of other countries simultaneously, and both only included the effect of smoking.
source: The two previous projections that incorporated both elements simultaneously only included the effect of smoking (Janssen et al., 2013; Li and Raftery, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janssen et al., 2013 and Li and Raftery, 2021.

claim: The approach developed by Janssen et al., 2013 consists of the combination of a coherent projection of non-smoking-related mortality with an age-period-cohort projection of smoking-attributable mortality.
source: The approach developed for this purpose by Janssen et al., 2013 consists of the combination of a coherent projection of non-smoking-related mortality with an age-period-cohort projection of smoking-attributable mortality.
evidence: This describes the methodology from a cited previous study.

claim: The approach by Janssen et al., 2013 was adopted by Statistics Netherlands as part of their official population forecast.
source: This approach was applied to the Netherlands (Janssen et al., 2013) and was adopted by Statistics Netherlands as part of their official population forecast (Stoeldraijer et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janssen et al., 2013 and Stoeldraijer et al., 2013b.

claim: Li and Raftery, 2021 applied an amended version of the Janssen et al., 2013 approach to 69 countries.
source: Li and Raftery, 2021 applied an amended version of this approach to 69 countries.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li and Raftery, 2021.

claim: The authors used existing recent age- and sex-specific estimates of mortality after excluding the combined impact of smoking, obesity, and alcohol from Janssen et al., 2021.
source: To this end, we used existing recent age- and sex-specific estimates of mortality after excluding the combined impact smoking, obesity, and alcohol (Janssen et al., 2021), which we refer to as non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
evidence: This describes the data source used in the methodology.

claim: The authors performed a Li-Lee coherent projection of non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: Specifically, we performed a Li–Lee coherent projection (Li and Lee, 2005) of non-lifestyle-attributable mortality in which we regarded the high life expectancy values and more favourable long-term trends among women in France, Spain, and Italy as the values and trends towards which the other populations will converge, since we regard these three populations as forerunners.
evidence: This describes the projection methodology used by the authors.

claim: The authors regarded women in France, Spain, and Italy as forerunner populations towards which other populations will converge.
source: Specifically, we performed a Li–Lee coherent projection (Li and Lee, 2005) of non-lifestyle-attributable mortality in which we regarded the high life expectancy values and more favourable long-term trends among women in France, Spain, and Italy as the values and trends towards which the other populations will converge, since we regard these three populations as forerunners.
evidence: This describes a key assumption in the authors' methodology.

claim: The authors utilized recently published projections of smoking-, obesity-, and alcohol-attributable mortality from Janssen et al., 2020c; Janssen et al., 2020b; and Janssen et al., 2020d.
source: We did so by utilizing recently published projections of smoking-, obesity-, and alcohol-attributable mortality that were both data and theory driven (Janssen et al., 2020c; Janssen et al., 2020b; Janssen et al., 2020d).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the methodology.

claim: The authors applied their projection approach to the national populations of 18 European countries.
source: We applied our projection approach to the national populations of 18 European countries (see Table 1 for the included countries)
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: The authors used country, sex, and age-specific all-cause mortality and exposure data for the 1990-2014 period from the Human Mortality Database.
source: using country, sex, and age-specific all-cause mortality and exposure data for the 1990–2014 period from the Human Mortality Database (HMD and University of California, Berkeley (USA), and Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research (Germany), 2019)
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: The authors were restricted in both the starting year and the end year because lifestyle-attributable mortality data was available only for the 1990-2014 period.
source: We were restricted in both the starting year and the end year because lifestyle-attributable mortality data was available only for this period.
evidence: This explains a limitation in the data availability.

claim: Over the 1990-2014 period, life expectancy at birth increased, on average, across the 18 European countries studied by 6.6 years for men (from 71.8 to 78.3 years) and by 4.8 years for women (from 78.6 to 83.4 years).
source: Over the 1990–2014 period, life expectancy at birth (e0) increased, on average, across the 18 European countries studied by 6.6 years for men (from 71.8 to 78.3 years) and by 4.8 years for women (from 78.6 to 83.4 years) (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' data analysis, supported by Table 1.

claim: The average yearly increase in life expectancy at birth over 1990-2014 was 0.28 years for men and 0.20 years for women.
source: These values translate into a yearly increase in e0 of 0.28 years for men and 0.20 years for women.
evidence: This is calculated from the observed data.

claim: Without the impact of smoking, obesity, and alcohol, the increase in life expectancy at birth over the 1990-2014 period was more similar between men (5.1 years; 0.21 annually) and women (5.3 years; 0.22 annually).
source: This difference between men and women can largely be attributed to lifestyle factors. Without the impact of smoking, obesity, and alcohol, the increase in e0 over the 1990–2014 period was more similar between men (5.1 years; 0.21 annually) and women (5.3 years; 0.22 annually).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.

claim: The increase in life expectancy at birth was more similar between countries for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality (variance: 0.5 for men, 0.6 for women) than for all-cause mortality (variance: 0.9 for men, 0.7 for women).
source: In addition, the increase in e0 was more similar between countries for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality (variance: 0.5 for men, 0.6 for women) than for all-cause mortality (variance: 0.9 for men, 0.7 for women).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' data analysis comparing variance across countries.

claim: The greater increase in life expectancy at birth for all-cause mortality than for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality among men can be explained by significant declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality men experienced.
source: The greater increase in e0 for all-cause mortality than for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality among men can be explained by the significant declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality men experienced (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by Figure 1.

claim: Declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality among men stemmed predominantly from large declines in smoking-attributable mortality.
source: These declines stemmed predominantly from large declines in smoking-attributable mortality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Past increases in lifestyle-attributable mortality among women were driven by increases in all three factors (except alcohol in Eastern Europe).
source: In contrast, the past increases in lifestyle-attributable mortality among women were driven by increases in all three factors (except alcohol in Eastern Europe) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Past increases in lifestyle-attributable mortality among women resulted in smaller increases in life expectancy at birth for all-cause mortality than for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: and resulted in smaller increases in e0 for all-cause mortality than for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on women's mortality trends.

claim: Trends in life expectancy at birth since 1950 have been rather unstable, whereas the trends in life expectancy at birth without lifestyle factors can be regarded as more stable.
source: Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 show that whereas trends in e0 since 1950 have been rather unstable, the trends in e0 without lifestyle factors can be regarded as more stable.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The more stable trend in life expectancy at birth for non-smoking-related mortality for men in the 1950s and 1960s seems to be in line with the more recent trends in life expectancy at birth for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: This is indicated by (1) the more stable trend in e0 for non-smoking-related mortality for men in the 1950s and 1960s, which seems to be in line with the more recent trends in e0 for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality
evidence: This is an observation from the figures showing historical trends.

claim: Among women, there is close correspondence between the recent trends in life expectancy at birth for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality and the trends in life expectancy at birth for all-cause mortality in the 1950s-1960s that were probably affected only minimally by lifestyle factors.
source: and (2) the close correspondence among women between the recent trends in e0 for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality and the trends in e0 for all-cause mortality in the 1950s–1960s that were probably affected only minimally by lifestyle factors.
evidence: This is an observation from the figures showing historical trends, with an inference about minimal lifestyle effects in the 1950s-1960s.

claim: For men, the past declines in age-standardised lifestyle-attributable mortality fractions over the 1990-2014 period are projected to further decline until 2065, albeit at a different pace than in the past.
source: For men, the past declines in age-standardised lifestyle-attributable mortality fractions (LAMF) over the 1990–2014 period are projected to further decline until 2065, albeit at a different pace than in the past.
evidence: This is a projection result from the authors' methodology.

claim: Among Eastern European men in particular, the decline in lifestyle-attributable mortality is projected to decelerate.
source: Among Eastern European men in particular, the decline is projected to decelerate.
evidence: This is a specific projection result for Eastern European men.

claim: For women, the authors project that the past increases in lifestyle-attributable mortality fractions will (eventually) turn into declines.
source: For women, we project that the past increases in LAMF will (eventually) turn into declines.
evidence: This is a projection result from the authors' methodology.

claim: The projections follow the observed wave-shaped dynamic of the smoking epidemic.
source: The projections follow the observed wave-shaped dynamic of the smoking epidemic (Lopez et al., 1994; Janssen, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lopez et al., 1994 and Janssen, 2020.

claim: The projections follow the hypothesised wave shape of the obesity epidemic.
source: and the hypothesised wave shape of the obesity epidemic (Xu and Lam, 2018; Jaacks et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu and Lam, 2018 and Jaacks et al., 2019.

claim: For alcohol-attributable mortality, unrealistic future differences between countries were avoided by assuming that the current increases observed for selected countries will eventually turn into declines.
source: For alcohol-attributable mortality, unrealistic future differences between countries were avoided by assuming that the current increases observed for selected countries will eventually turn into declines (Janssen et al., 2020d).
evidence: This describes an assumption made in the projection methodology, supported by a citation to Janssen et al., 2020d.

claim: The projected average increase per year in life expectancy at birth is 0.24 years for men and 0.18 years for women.
source: This represents an average increase per year of 0.24 years for men and 0.18 years for women.
evidence: This is calculated from the projected life expectancy values.

claim: The projected increase in life expectancy at birth is greater for men than for women because all-cause mortality levels are currently further away from non-lifestyle-attributable mortality levels for men than for women.
source: The projected increase is greater for men than for women because all-cause mortality levels are currently further away from non-lifestyle-attributable mortality levels for men than for women and because lifestyle-attributable mortality is higher among men than among women.
evidence: This is an explanation provided by the authors for their projection results.

claim: Lifestyle-attributable mortality is higher among men than among women.
source: and because lifestyle-attributable mortality is higher among men than among women.
evidence: This is stated as a fact based on the data.

claim: There is more room for improvement in life expectancy for men than for women.
source: There is, therefore, more room for improvement for men than for women.
evidence: This is an inference from the previous claims about mortality levels.

claim: The sex difference in life expectancy at birth is projected to decline from, on average, 5.0 years in 2014 to 2.3 years in 2065.
source: The sex difference in e0 is projected to decline from, on average, 5.0 years in 2014 to 2.3 years in 2065 (Supplementary file 1A; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a projection result supported by Supplementary file 1A and Figure 3.

claim: The gap in life expectancy at birth is projected to be smallest in Greece, at 1.5 years.
source: The gap is projected to be smallest in Greece, at 1.5 years
evidence: This is a specific projection result for Greece.

claim: The gap in life expectancy at birth is projected to be largest in Slovenia, at 2.7 years.
source: and largest in Slovenia, at 2.7 years.
evidence: This is a specific projection result for Slovenia.

claim: The sex differences in life expectancy are smaller for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality than for all-cause mortality.
source: Among the explanations for the projected convergence of the sex gap in e0 is that the sex differences are smaller for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality than for all-cause mortality
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the projected convergence.

claim: The sex differences in lifestyle-attributable mortality are smaller in the long run.
source: the sex differences in lifestyle-attributable mortality are smaller in the long run
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the projected convergence.

claim: The authors' projection results in higher future life expectancy at birth in 2065 for all populations under study compared to the benchmark Lee-Carter extrapolative mortality projection.
source: Compared to the benchmark Lee–Carter (LC) extrapolative mortality projection, our projection results in higher future e0 in 2065 for all populations under study (Table 2).
evidence: This is a comparison result supported by Table 2.

claim: On average, the projected life expectancy at birth values in 2065 are 2.6 years higher for men and 2.1 years higher for women in the authors' projection than in the individual Lee-Carter mortality projection.
source: On average, the projected e0 values in 2065 are 2.6 years higher for men and 2.1 years higher for women in our projection than in the individual Lee–Carter mortality projection, which projected e0 values of 87.9 years for men and 90.6 years for women in 2065 (Table 2).
evidence: This is a comparison result supported by Table 2.

claim: The Lee-Carter projection projects life expectancy at birth values of 87.9 years for men and 90.6 years for women in 2065.
source: which projected e0 values of 87.9 years for men and 90.6 years for women in 2065 (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the Lee-Carter projection, supported by Table 2.

claim: For men, particularly in Hungary, the differences between the authors' projected values and those of the Lee-Carter projection are considerable, mainly because of large projected declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: For men, particularly in Hungary, the differences between our projected values and those of the LC projection are considerable, mainly because of large projected declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality.
evidence: This is an explanation for the differences observed in the comparison.

claim: For Dutch women, a considerable difference between the authors' projection and the Lee-Carter projection can be observed.
source: Also for Dutch women a considerable difference between our projection and the LC projection can be observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison results.

claim: For Dutch women, not only large declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality are projected, but they also experienced a more favourable trend in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality than in all-cause mortality.
source: For Dutch women not only large declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality are projected, but they also experienced a more favourable trend in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality than in all-cause mortality.
evidence: This is an explanation for the differences observed for Dutch women.

claim: The authors' projection results in smaller differences in future life expectancy at birth between countries and sexes compared to the Lee-Carter projection.
source: In addition, our projection results in smaller differences in future e0 between countries and sexes.
evidence: This is a comparison result.

claim: The Lee-Carter projection projects that the variance between countries in life expectancy at birth for 2065 is 3.8 years for men and 1.7 years for women.
source: That is, the LC projection projects that the variance between countries in e0 for 2065 is 3.8 years for men and 1.7 years for women
evidence: This is a result from the Lee-Carter projection.

claim: In the authors' projection, the expected variance in life expectancy at birth between countries for 2065 is 0.6 years for both men and women.
source: whereas in our projection, the expected variance is 0.6 years for both men and women (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the authors' projection, supported by Table 2.

claim: The Lee-Carter projection can result in unlikely crossovers and divergences between countries.
source: In addition, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 illustrates that the LC projection, unlike our projection, can result in unlikely crossovers and divergences between countries (e.g., Greece and Hungary for men; the Netherlands and Slovenia for women).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sex difference in life expectancy at birth in 2065 is projected to be 2.7 years in the Lee-Carter projection.
source: In addition, the sex difference in e0 in 2065 is projected to be 2.7 years in the LC projection
evidence: This is a result from the Lee-Carter projection.

claim: The sex difference in life expectancy at birth in 2065 is projected to be 2.3 years in the authors' projection.
source: but 2.3 years in our projection (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the authors' projection, supported by Table 2.

claim: The Lee-Carter projection reveals large differences in the projected sex differences in life expectancy at birth between countries ranging from 0.1 to 5.4 years.
source: Furthermore, a closer look at the sex differences projected by the LC projection (Supplementary file 1A) reveals large differences in the projected sex differences between countries ranging from 0.1 to 5.4 years.
evidence: This is an observation from the Lee-Carter projection results, supported by Supplementary file 1A.

claim: In the authors' projection, the range of projected sex differences in life expectancy at birth between countries is between 1.5 and 2.7 years.
source: In our projection, by contrast, the range is between 1.5 and 2.7 years.
evidence: This is a result from the authors' projection.

claim: The very small difference in life expectancy at birth between women and men projected for 2065 in the Netherlands (0.1 years) and in the United Kingdom (0.9 years) by the Lee-Carter projection indicates that the individual Lee-Carter projection of all-cause mortality might result in an unlikely crossover between men and women in life expectancy at birth in the long-term future.
source: The very small difference in e0 between women and men projected for 2065 in the Netherlands (0.1 years) and in the United Kingdom (0.9 years) indicates that the individual LC projection of all-cause mortality might result in an unlikely crossover between men and women in e0 in the long-term future due to the more favourable past trends in all-cause mortality among men than among women in the 1990–2014 period.
evidence: This is an inference from the Lee-Carter projection results.

claim: The authors' projection avoids an unlikely crossover in future life expectancy values between men and women.
source: Thus, our projection avoids an unlikely crossover in future life expectancy values between men and women.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the authors' projection approach.

claim: Unlike the Lee-Carter mortality projection, the authors' projection results in non-linear future increases in life expectancy at birth.
source: Moreover, unlike the LC mortality projection, our projection results in non-linear future increases in e0 (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: For men in Belgium, Greece, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland, and for women in Hungary, Denmark, and the United Kingdom, the authors project faster increases in life expectancy in the early decades, but slower increases in life expectancy further in the future.
source: Particularly for men in Belgium, Greece, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Poland, but also for women in Hungary, Denmark, and the United Kingdom, we see faster projected increases in life expectancy in the early decades, but slower increases in life expectancy further in the future, in line with the projections of lifestyle-attributable mortality.
evidence: This is a specific projection result for certain countries.

claim: The Lee-Carter projection anticipates more constant future increases in life expectancy at birth.
source: The LC projection, by contrast, anticipates more constant future increases in life expectancy at birth.
evidence: This is a characterization of the Lee-Carter projection results.

claim: The higher values estimated by the authors' projection than by the Lee-Carter projection stem from both the lifestyle dimension and the coherent dimension.
source: The higher values estimated by our projection than by the LC projection stem from both dimensions (Table 2; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is an explanation for the differences, supported by Table 2 and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The coherent dimension led to higher values because the French, Italian, and Spanish women combined exhibited more favourable trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality than the individual populations combined, after controlling for the underlying age pattern of mortality.
source: The coherent dimension led to higher values because the French, Italian, and Spanish women combined exhibited more favourable trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality than the individual populations combined, after controlling for the underlying age pattern of mortality.
evidence: This is an explanation for the effect of the coherent dimension.

claim: For women, unlike for men, the past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality were more favourable than the past trends in all-cause mortality.
source: For women, unlike for men, the past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality were more favourable than the past trends in all-cause mortality.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: For both men and women, an additional positive effect emerges from the projected (eventual) decline in lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: For both men and women, an additional positive effect emerges from the projected (eventual) decline in lifestyle-attributable mortality.
evidence: This is an explanation for the higher projected values.

claim: The smaller projected differences between countries in the authors' projection than in the Lee-Carter projection stem from both the lifestyle and coherent elements, although for men, the impact of integrating lifestyle is more pronounced.
source: The smaller projected differences between countries in our projection than in the LC projection also stem from both elements, although for men, the impact of integrating lifestyle is more pronounced (Table 2; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is an explanation for the differences, supported by Table 2 and Supplementary file 1B.

claim: For men, the past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality were much more similar between countries than the past trends in all-cause mortality.
source: Particularly for men, the past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality were much more similar between countries than the past trends in all-cause mortality.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: For both men and women, country differences in lifestyle-attributable mortality in 2065 are projected to be smaller than they are currently.
source: In addition, for both men and women, country differences in lifestyle-attributable mortality in 2065 are projected to be smaller than they are currently.
evidence: This is a projection result.

claim: The smaller sex differences in projected life expectancy at birth values in the authors' projection stem purely from the convergence dimension.
source: The smaller sex differences in projected e0 values in our projection stem purely from the convergence dimension
evidence: This is an explanation for the smaller sex differences.

claim: The nonlinearity of future trends in the authors' projection stems completely from the lifestyle dimension.
source: whereas the nonlinearity of future trends in our projection stems completely from the lifestyle dimension.
evidence: This is an explanation for the nonlinearity.

claim: The inclusion of the lifestyle dimension in the Lee-Carter projection leads to a future life expectancy at birth that is moving back upwards towards the future trend in life expectancy at birth for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: Figure 3—figure supplement 3 illustrates that the inclusion of the lifestyle dimension in the Lee–Carter projection (thus ignoring the coherent dimension) leads to a future e0 that is moving back upwards towards the future trend in e0 for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality serve as a better approximation of the underlying mortality trend than past trends in all-cause mortality.
source: An important element of our projection approach is the identification of the underlying long-term mortality trend that can be extrapolated into the future. We illustrated that past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality serve this purpose better than past trends in all-cause mortality.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the authors' analysis.

claim: For non-lifestyle-attributable mortality, the differences in past trends between countries and between men and women are smaller, and the trends are more robust.
source: For non-lifestyle-attributable mortality, the differences in past trends between countries and between men and women are smaller, and the trends are more robust.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' data analysis.

claim: The trends in all-cause mortality exhibit a wave-shaped fluctuation due to initial increases in smoking-, obesity-, and alcohol-attributable mortality, followed (eventually) by declines.
source: In contrast, the trends in all-cause mortality exhibit a wave-shaped fluctuation due to initial increases in smoking-, obesity-, and alcohol-attributable mortality, followed (eventually) by declines.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Extrapolating past declines in all-cause mortality will lead to non-reliable outcomes: i.e., the outcomes will be either too low when decelerating increases are extrapolated or too high when accelerating increases are extrapolated.
source: Thus, extrapolating past declines in all-cause mortality will lead to non-reliable outcomes: i.e., the outcomes will be either too low when decelerating increases are extrapolated or too high when accelerating increases are extrapolated.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the wave-shaped pattern of all-cause mortality trends.

claim: The extrapolation of past trends in all-cause mortality will result in non-robust outcomes when updating the projection after a few years.
source: Similarly, the extrapolation of past trends in all-cause mortality will result in non-robust outcomes, when updating the projection after a few years.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the instability of all-cause mortality trends.

claim: Because the past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality are more linear than the past trends in all-cause mortality, especially from a historical point of view, the authors' projection is less dependent on the data period used for the extrapolation.
source: Because the past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality are more linear than the past trends in all-cause mortality, especially from a historical point of view, our projection is less dependent on the data period used for the extrapolation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the linearity of non-lifestyle-attributable mortality trends.

claim: The average annual past increase in life expectancy at birth for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality of 0.21 years for men and 0.22 years for women across the 18 European countries over the 1990-2014 period is lower than the continuous upward trend in record life expectancy of 0.243 years that Oeppen and Vaupel, 2002 observed over the 1840-2000 period.
source: Our finding of an average annual past increase in e0 for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality of 0.21 years for men and 0.22 years for women across the 18 European countries over the 1990–2014 period is lower than the continuous upward trend in record life expectancy of 0.243 years that Oeppen and Vaupel, 2002 observed over the 1840–2000 period.
evidence: This is a comparison with a finding from Oeppen and Vaupel, 2002.

claim: Record life expectancy values always increase, but the levels in individual countries may not.
source: First, whereas record values always increase, the levels in individual countries may not
evidence: This is a logical statement about the nature of record values.

claim: Since the 1990s, the record life expectancy has been observed for a non-European country (Japan).
source: and since the 1990s, the record life expectancy has been observed for a non-European country (Japan).
evidence: This is a factual statement about record life expectancy.

claim: More recent increases in life expectancy are driven more by declines in mortality from chronic diseases at older ages with a less strong effect on life expectancy than from declines in mortality from infectious diseases at younger ages, which drove increases in life expectancy up to 1950.
source: Second, more recent increases in life expectancy are driven more by declines in mortality from chronic diseases at older ages with a less strong effect on life expectancy than from declines in mortality from infectious diseases at younger ages, which drove increases in life expectancy up to 1950 (Omran, 1998; Vallin and Meslé, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Omran, 1998 and Vallin and Meslé, 2009.

claim: A deceleration of increases in life expectancy over time is inevitable.
source: As a result, a deceleration of increases in life expectancy over time is inevitable.
evidence: This is an inference from the shift in causes of mortality decline.

claim: Large past increases in life expectancy at birth for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality indicate that considerable increases in life expectancy at birth are likely in the future.
source: Nonetheless, these large past increases in e0 for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality indicate that considerable increases in e0 are likely in the future.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed past trends.

claim: The authors applied a coherent mortality projection approach to past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: We applied a coherent mortality projection approach to past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
evidence: This describes the methodology used.

claim: The coherent mortality projection approach resulted in more realistic estimates of the differences in future life expectancy at birth values between countries and sexes than those of the individual Lee-Carter projection of past trends.
source: This resulted in more realistic estimates of the differences in future e0 values between countries and sexes than those of the individual Lee–Carter projection of past trends.
evidence: This is a comparison result.

claim: The inclusion of the mortality experiences of other countries in the projection provided a broader empirical basis for the determination of the most likely future developments.
source: Another added value of our inclusion of the mortality experiences of other countries in our projection is that it provided a broader empirical basis for the determination of the most likely future developments (Janssen and Kunst, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Janssen and Kunst, 2007.

claim: The inclusion of the mortality experiences of other countries improved the robustness of the projection outcomes.
source: which, in turn, improved the robustness of our projection outcomes (Stoeldraijer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stoeldraijer, 2019.

claim: Using forerunner populations as the reference population will generally result in higher future life expectancy values than using an average across many populations.
source: Using forerunner populations as the reference population, as advocated by among others Oeppen and Vaupel, 2002 and Bergeron-Boucher et al., 2018, instead of an average across many populations (Li and Lee, 2005; Eurostat, 2020a) will generally result in higher future life expectancy values (see the next section as well).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oeppen and Vaupel, 2002; Bergeron-Boucher et al., 2018; Li and Lee, 2005; and Eurostat, 2020a.

claim: The past trend in life expectancy at birth for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality is more equal between countries and sexes than the past trend in life expectancy at birth for all-cause mortality.
source: However, given that the past trend in e0 for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality is more equal between countries and sexes than the past trend in e0 for all-cause mortality (see Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by Table 1.

claim: Which reference populations are chosen will likely have a larger impact when coherently forecasting all-cause mortality than when coherently forecasting non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: which reference populations are chosen will likely have a larger impact when coherently forecasting all-cause mortality than when coherently forecasting non-lifestyle-attributable mortality (see also Janssen and Kunst, 2007 and Janssen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Janssen and Kunst, 2007 and Janssen et al., 2013.

claim: The authors' convergence assumption relies on at least a continuation of improvements in socio-economic developments and medical care.
source: In addition, our convergence assumption relies on – at least – a continuation of improvements in socio-economic developments and medical care.
evidence: This describes an assumption underlying the projection.

claim: Continued improvements in socio-economic developments and medical care depend on continued investments in these areas, including diminishing socio-economic inequalities, better preparations for additional possible outbreaks of infectious diseases, and for the potential harmful effects of climate change.
source: Such continued improvements depend on continued investments in these areas, including diminishing socio-economic inequalities, better preparations for additional possible outbreaks of infectious diseases, and for the potential harmful effects of climate change.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the conditions necessary for continued improvements.

claim: The authors' assumption of continued improvements is supported by evidence that life expectancy has long followed a continuously increasing trend.
source: Although this might be considered optimistic, our assumption is supported by evidence that life expectancy has long followed a continuously increasing trend (Oeppen and Vaupel, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oeppen and Vaupel, 2002.

claim: The continuously increasing trend in life expectancy is even stronger from a historical perspective if the effects of lifestyle factors are excluded.
source: and that this trend is even stronger from a historical perspective if the effects of lifestyle factors are excluded (see the description of Figure 2 and its supplement in the Results section).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2 and its supplement.

claim: The underlying long-term mortality decline is argued not to be affected by COVID-19.
source: Second, the underlying long-term mortality decline is argued not to be affected by COVID-19 (e.g., Stoeldraijer, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stoeldraijer, 2020.

claim: The predominant temporal dip in life expectancy as a result of the Spanish flu in 1918 supports the argument that the underlying long-term mortality decline is not affected by COVID-19.
source: in line with the predominant temporal dip in life expectancy as a result of the Spanish flu in 1918 (see Roser, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roser, 2020.

claim: The continuation of the underlying long-term mortality decline depends on important investments to achieve continued improvements in socio-economic developments and medical care.
source: Although, as mentioned, the continuation of the underlying long-term mortality decline does depend on important investments to achieve continued improvements in socio-economic developments and medical care.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the conditions necessary for continued decline.

claim: The authors' findings of higher projected life expectancy values than those estimated by the benchmark Lee-Carter mortality projection and the official mortality forecasts by Eurostat and the United Nations have important implications for society.
source: Our findings of higher projected life expectancy values than those estimated by the benchmark Lee–Carter mortality projection and the official mortality forecasts by Eurostat and the United Nations have important implications for society.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Individuals could consider planning their life course (e.g., education, work) differently given their longer expected lifespan.
source: First, individuals could consider planning their life course (e.g., education, work) differently given their longer expected lifespan.
evidence: This is a potential implication of the findings.

claim: A higher projected life expectancy suggests that there will be more older people in the population, which will likely bring both opportunities (e.g., an experienced workforce) and challenges in terms of healthcare planning and social security.
source: Second, a higher projected life expectancy suggests that there will be more older people in the population, which will likely bring both opportunities (e.g., an experienced workforce) and challenges in terms of healthcare planning and social security.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of higher life expectancy.

claim: The authors' results imply that either the pension age will have to be raised or, if it is not, that the capital requirements of pension providers will need to be increased.
source: Our results imply that either the pension age will have to be raised or, if it is not, that the capital requirements of pension providers will need to be increased.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications for pension systems.

claim: For determining the pension age based on projected life expectancy, a projection that is more robust will have significant added value.
source: For determining the pension age based on projected life expectancy, a projection that is more robust will have significant added value.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the value of robust projections.

claim: Having a more stable projection of mortality will allow for more robust population forecasts.
source: More generally, having a more stable projection of mortality will allow for more robust population forecasts.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the value of stable projections.

claim: The authors' findings of higher projected life expectancy values than those currently used in most mortality projection methodologies and of a rather robust long-term increase in life expectancy at birth after the effects of smoking, obesity, and alcohol are controlled for, indicate that a limit to human life expectancy (average lifespan) is not within reach.
source: In addition, our findings of (1) higher projected life expectancy values than those currently used in most mortality projection methodologies and (2) of a rather robust long-term increase in e0 after the effects of smoking, obesity, and alcohol are controlled for, indicate that a limit to human life expectancy (average lifespan) is not within reach – an issue that continues to spark scientific debate (see the first paragraph of the introduction).
evidence: This is an inference from the findings about the debate on limits to life expectancy.

claim: Compared to the most recent official mortality forecast by Eurostat, 2020a and the United Nations, 2020, the authors' mortality projection resulted in substantially higher projected life expectancy at birth values in 2065.
source: Moreover, compared to the most recent official mortality forecast by Eurostat, 2020a and the United Nations, 2020, our mortality projection resulted in substantially higher projected e0 values in 2065 (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a comparison result supported by Supplementary file 1C.

claim: The authors' projected life expectancy at birth values in 2065 were, on average, 5.0 years higher for men and 3.2 years (Eurostat) and 4.3 years (UN) higher for women compared to Eurostat and UN projections.
source: Our values were, on average, 5.0 years higher for men and 3.2 years (Eurostat) and 4.3 years (UN) higher for women.
evidence: This is a comparison result.

claim: The UN projects very large and unrealistic differences in future life expectancy between countries and sexes, including higher projected life expectancy for men than for women in a number of countries.
source: The UN projects very large and unrealistic differences in future life expectancy between countries and sexes, including higher projected life expectancy for men than for women in a number of countries.
evidence: This is a characterization of the UN projection results.

claim: The UN projection outcomes clearly show the added value of adopting a coherent mortality projection approach.
source: These outcomes clearly show the added value of adopting a coherent mortality projection approach.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison with UN projections.

claim: Eurostat has performed a coherent mortality projection using a different methodology.
source: While Eurostat has performed a coherent mortality projection, it used a different methodology.
evidence: This is a statement about Eurostat's methodology.

claim: Eurostat made a partial convergence assumption, applied to men and women separately, and considered the aggregate all-cause mortality of 12 countries as the target.
source: Eurostat made a partial convergence assumption, applied to men and women separately, and considered the aggregate all-cause mortality of 12 countries (Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Finland, Sweden, and the United Kingdom) as the target (Lanzieri, 2009; Eurostat, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lanzieri, 2009 and Eurostat, 2020b.

claim: Eurostat did not integrate the role of lifestyle factors in their projection.
source: In addition, Eurostat did not integrate the role of lifestyle factors.
evidence: This is a statement about what Eurostat's projection did not include.

claim: The added value of the authors' projection approach over pure coherent mortality forecasting is that they projected the more robust past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality rather than in all-cause mortality, and they projected non-linear future trends in line with the projection of lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: The added value of our projection approach over pure coherent mortality forecasting is that we projected the more robust past trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality rather than in all-cause mortality, and we projected non-linear future trends in line with the projection of lifestyle-attributable mortality.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the authors' approach.

claim: Coherent mortality projections have to be applied to non-lifestyle-attributable mortality rather than to all-cause mortality because there are important differences in smoking-, obesity-, and alcohol-attributable mortality trends between countries and sexes.
source: The reason why coherent mortality projections have to be applied to non-lifestyle-attributable mortality rather than to all-cause mortality is that there are important differences in smoking-, obesity-, and alcohol-attributable mortality trends between countries and sexes (Janssen, 2020; Vidra et al., 2019; Janssen et al., 2020d).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janssen, 2020; Vidra et al., 2019; and Janssen et al., 2020d.

claim: Among the advantages of taking the effects of obesity and alcohol in addition to those of smoking into account is that life expectancy at birth values for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality are higher than life expectancy at birth values for non-smoking-attributable mortality, and thus have the potential for larger future increases.
source: Among the advantages of taking the effects of obesity and alcohol in addition to those of smoking into account is that e0 values for non-lifestyle-attributable mortality are higher than e0 values for non-smoking-attributable mortality (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and thus have the potential for larger future increases.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effects of both obesity-attributable mortality and alcohol-attributable mortality (particularly among Eastern European men) on past and future life expectancy trends are large.
source: In addition, as was illustrated, the effects of both obesity-attributable mortality and alcohol-attributable mortality (particularly among Eastern European men) on past and future life expectancy trends are large.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The outcomes of the authors' projection approach can be considered more realistic, more robust, and more insightful than previous extrapolative mortality projections, including those by the United Nations and Eurostat.
source: All in all, the outcomes of our projection approach, which simultaneously takes into account the lifestyle factors smoking, obesity and alcohol, and the mortality experiences of forerunner populations, can be considered more realistic, more robust, and more insightful than previous extrapolative mortality projections, including those by the United Nations and Eurostat.
evidence: This is the authors' overall conclusion about their approach.

claim: The authors' approach, which distinguishes between the underlying long-term mortality decline and the remaining factors that cause deviations from this mortality decline, could also be adopted to account for the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on mortality and life expectancy.
source: Our approach, which distinguishes between the underlying long-term mortality decline and the remaining factors that cause deviations from this mortality decline, could also be adopted to account for the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on mortality and life expectancy.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future application of the approach.

claim: It would be illogical to extrapolate the mortality trends up to 2020 to obtain life expectancy estimates for 2021 and beyond, because life expectancy in 2020 has been importantly negatively affected by COVID-19.
source: First, it would be illogical to extrapolate the mortality trends up to 2020 to obtain life expectancy estimates for 2021 and beyond, because life expectancy in 2020 has been importantly negatively affected by COVID-19 (Marois et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marois et al., 2020.

claim: Life expectancy in 2020 has been importantly negatively affected by COVID-19, and will likely continue to be so for at least 2021.
source: and will likely to continue to do so for at least 2021.
evidence: This is a speculation about the continued impact of COVID-19.

claim: The effect of COVID-19 on life expectancy cannot be predicted using a simple extrapolation approach.
source: This effect cannot be predicted using a simple extrapolation approach.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the limitations of extrapolation.

claim: The highest life expectancy at birth in 2065 is projected for France among women (94.0) and for Italy among men (91.4).
source: The highest e0 in 2065 is projected for France among women (94.0) and for Italy among men (91.4).
evidence: This is a specific projection result.

claim: Hungary is the country with the lowest projected life expectancy at birth in 2065, at 88.6 years among men and 91.0 years among women.
source: Hungary is the country with the lowest projected e0 in 2065, at 88.6 years among men and 91.0 years among women.
evidence: This is a specific projection result.

claim: France and Italy had the (second) highest life expectancy at birth values in 2014, and Hungary had the lowest.
source: These countries also had in 2014, respectively, the (second) highest and the lowest values.
evidence: This is an observation from the 2014 data.

claim: The authors project the largest gains in life expectancy for Hungary and Poland, particularly among men.
source: We project the largest gains in life expectancy for Hungary and Poland, particularly among men
evidence: This is a projection result.

claim: The largest gains in life expectancy for Hungary and Poland are in line with past large increases in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality due to a process of catch-up, and large projected declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality in these countries.
source: in line with past large increases in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality due to a process of catch-up (Table 1), and large projected declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality in these countries (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an explanation for the projected gains, supported by Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Among women, the authors project large gains in life expectancy for Denmark and the United Kingdom.
source: Among women, we project large gains as well for Denmark and the United Kingdom
evidence: This is a projection result.

claim: The large gains in life expectancy for Denmark and the United Kingdom among women can be attributed to their high current levels of lifestyle-attributable mortality, predominantly due to their high levels of smoking-attributable mortality, and the large projected (continued) declines therein.
source: which can be attributed to their high current levels of lifestyle-attributable mortality, predominantly due to their high levels of smoking-attributable mortality, and the large projected (continued) declines therein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an explanation for the projected gains, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The smallest gains in life expectancy are projected for Switzerland.
source: The smallest gains are projected for Switzerland
evidence: This is a projection result.

claim: The smallest gains in life expectancy for Switzerland could be related to the relatively small projected declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality resulting from a long projected continuation of increases in obesity prevalence.
source: which could be related to the relatively small projected declines in lifestyle-attributable mortality resulting from a long projected continuation of increases in obesity prevalence.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the projected gains.

claim: The projection of lifestyle-attributable mortality involves more subjectivity than the extrapolation of non-lifestyle-attributable mortality.
source: Nonetheless, the projection of lifestyle-attributable mortality involves more subjectivity than the extrapolation of non-lifestyle-attributable mortality (see Janssen et al., 2020c; Janssen et al., 2020b; Janssen et al., 2020d for a critical evaluation).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Janssen et al., 2020c; Janssen et al., 2020b; and Janssen et al., 2020d.

claim: In the separate projections of smoking-, obesity-, and alcohol-attributable mortality, population-specific lower bounds were implemented to avoid unlikely future estimates of zero smoking, obesity, and alcohol prevalence.
source: For example, in the separate projections of smoking-, obesity-, and alcohol-attributable mortality, population-specific lower bounds were implemented to avoid unlikely future estimates of zero smoking, obesity, and alcohol prevalence, in line with the theory (Lopez et al., 1994; Xu and Lam, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lopez et al., 1994 and Xu and Lam, 2018.

claim: Population-specific lower bounds were implemented to prevent unlikely crossovers between sexes and between countries in alcohol-attributable mortality.
source: and to prevent unlikely crossovers between sexes and between countries in alcohol-attributable mortality.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to avoid unrealistic outcomes.

claim: The use of population-specific lower bounds in projections could be considered conservative.
source: This approach could be considered conservative.
evidence: This is an evaluation of the methodological choice.

claim: The use of a wave-shaped pattern for obesity, and the large declines in alcohol-attributable mortality projected for Eastern European countries, could be considered too optimistic.
source: On the other hand, however, the use of a wave-shaped pattern for obesity, and the large declines in alcohol-attributable mortality we project for Eastern European countries, could be considered too optimistic.
evidence: This is an evaluation of the methodological choices.

claim: The added value of integrating lifestyle into mortality projections outweighs the uncertainties that come with it.
source: However, in our view, the added value of integrating lifestyle into mortality projections outweighs the uncertainties that come with it.
evidence: This is the authors' opinion about their approach.

claim: Trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality provide a better approximation of the underlying mortality trend.
source: First, trends in non-lifestyle-attributable mortality provide a better approximation of the underlying mortality trend.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the approach.

claim: The authors' projection is driven not only by data, but also by theory, and is preceded by a careful study of past trends.
source: Second, our projection is driven not only by data, but also by theory, and is preceded by a careful study of past trends.
evidence: This describes the basis of the projection approach.

claim: By distinguishing between the underlying mortality trend and the additional effect of the three lifestyle factors combined, the projections provide much greater transparency and insight than a mere mechanical extrapolation of past trends could.
source: Third, by distinguishing between the underlying mortality trend and the additional effect of the three lifestyle factors combined, these projections provide much greater transparency and insight than a mere mechanical extrapolation of past trends could.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the approach.

claim: The authors' approach resulted in more realistic differences between countries and sexes than those projected by other approaches.
source: Fourth, our approach resulted in more realistic differences between countries and sexes than those projected by other approaches (see the next section as well).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the approach.

claim: The four added values of the authors' mortality projection approach can be clearly linked to important criteria for evaluating the performance of mortality forecasts: namely, robustness, plausibility, reasonableness, and transparency.
source: The abovementioned four added values of our mortality projection approach can be clearly linked to important criteria for evaluating the performance of mortality forecasts in addition to accuracy: namely, robustness, plausibility, reasonableness, and transparency (Cairns et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cairns et al., 2009.

claim: The outcomes of the authors' projection approach are less dependent on the explicit choices that underlie general mortality forecasts (e.g., the choice of the forerunner populations and the historical time period).
source: Moreover, the outcomes of our projection approach – which rely above all on the coherent projection of non-lifestyle-attributable mortality – are less dependent on the explicit choices that underlie general mortality forecasts (e.g., the choice of the forerunner populations and the historical time period).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the approach.
